docs.task: How Layer 1 guards are defined, ordered, and tested in ostra-policy, and how a denial reason is written.

asks: How Layer 1 guards are defined in ostra-policy
How a denial reason is written

data_flow.step: An executor (native loop, or a harness adapter after translating its payload to canonical Claude Code names) calls `ExecutionPolicy::check(&ToolCall)`. For a Bash call it parses the command once with `bash::parse`.

`check` calls `layer1(call, parsed)`. A `Some(Denial)` returns at once through `from_denial`, which maps it to `PolicyDecision::Deny { reason, rule }`. Layer 2 and YOLO are never reached, so nothing overrides a guard.

`layer1` snapshots the build-streak state (pending recovery, blocked flag, streak count, last signature) under the mutex, then runs guards in a fixed order. First denial wins. Order, with early returns marked: (1) `answer_only` runs: any write path, Report, Document, Memory, manage tool, or shell write target is refused with `answer-only`; (2) tool `Report`: refused with `lesson-gate` if a recovery is pending and `reason` is empty, otherwise returns None (early return); (3) tool `Document`: returns `guards::check_document` (early return); (4) manage tools (ProjectCreate and kin): returns `guards::check_manage` (early return); (5) `owes_reply` and a `submit_*` tool: `reply-first` (Rule H3); (6) any other `submit_*`: `lesson-gate` when status is `ok` and a recovery is pending, else None (early return); (7) `PowerShell`/`Cmd`: `check_opaque_shell`; (8) for each path from `write_paths` (Write, Edit, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit, ApplyPatch): `check_write`; (9) a file tool's `read_path`: `check_windows_path`, then `check_read` (`secret-read`); (10) when `self.sandboxed`: `check_ignored_search_tool` for Grep and Glob, and `check_ignored_search_shell` for Bash (`ignored-search`, Rule G2); (11) for Bash: `check_shell`, then `check_shell_reads`, then for each `shell_targets` entry `check_ambiguous_target` then `check_write`; (12) last, the build-streak gate for a Bash command that `build::is_build_command` matches.

`check_write` is itself an ordered list, run once per write target (Write/Edit path or shell redirect/cp/rm target): `check_creates_project` (manage-tools, Rule O2); `check_windows_path` (windows-path); self-protection when `roots.strict` and the target is protected; workspace-artifacts (W1); workspace-docs (B5); git-metadata (any `.git` component); state-ownership (engine state, then TOOL_OWNED names, then AGENT_OWNED names for non-owners); artifact-ownership (ARTIFACTS regexes, skipped under a `factcheck-snapshot-*` ancestor); document-tool (target in the session dir that `doc_kind_for` recognizes); `check_scope` (`no-tests-from-implementer` first, then, only when `roots.strict`: quick-answer read-only, session-dir and repo-root scope, per-agent roots, session-only agents); finally report-path (only when `roots.report_file` is set, the target is inside the session root and named `ostra-*`; refused when `strict` and the path is not the declared one, then `lesson-gate` if a recovery is pending).

A Denial's `rule` is `RuleRef::guard(<const>)` with layer `guard`, and its `reason` is the model-facing text. The native executor shows the model ``Denied by guard `build-streak`: ...`` and the hook bridge appends `(Ostra guard: build-streak)`; the Activity view shows the rule next to each call (docs/security/agent-containment.md, 'Why a denial leads with the correction'). The Grok adapter passes the reason through `fit_reason`.

patterns.description: A guard is a `pub fn check_*` (or private helper) in guards.rs that takes the execution context and/or `Roots` plus a target and returns `Some(Denial)` to refuse or `None` to pass. A guard id is a `pub const &str` at the top of the file. The private `deny(guard, reason)` builds the Denial with `RuleRef::guard(guard)`. There is no trait, list, or registry of guards. The file's doc comment says each guard ports an Ultracode hook library, and each function's comment names its source (for example `(scope-policy.js checkScope)`, `(ledger-policy.js)`) or a Rule ID (`Rule W1`, `Rule B5`, `Rule O2`, `Rule G1`, `Rule G2`, `Rule H3`), or `Hardening:` for Ostra-only additions.
patterns.name: Guard as a free function returning Option<Denial>

patterns.description: Rule W1 (workspace-artifacts) and Rule B5 (workspace-docs) are two-condition guards placed inside `check_write`. A guard that applies only with tool enforcement checks `roots.strict` (Rule G1: `roots.strict` is false when `tool_enforcement` is disabled); guards that must hold in every mode do not test it. `check_read` is a standalone guard that is a single `then`.
patterns.name: A small guard in full, with its rule citation and enforcement toggle

patterns.description: A guard that is not about a write target is a `pub fn check_*` called from `ExecutionPolicy::layer1` in policy.rs. Examples: `check_read` (Hardening), `check_windows_path`, `check_ignored_search_tool`, `check_shell`, `check_shell_reads`, `check_opaque_shell`. Guards that need execution state held in `ExecutionPolicy` (the build streak, the pending lesson) are written inline in layer1 and build their Denial directly (`Denial { rule: RuleRef::guard(guards::BUILD_STREAK), reason: format!(...) }`), or call a public helper such as `guards::lesson_denial` / `answer_only_denial` / `reply_first_denial`. The build-streak guard is the only guard whose message is built in policy.rs.
patterns.name: Standalone check function plus a hook in layer1

patterns.description: All guard tests are integration tests in crates/ostra-policy/tests/policy.rs. `fx()` builds a temp tree under CARGO_TARGET_TMPDIR with `repo/src`, a session dir, `bin/ostra`, and `config/config.toml`; `Fx::ctx(agent)` returns an ExecContext with `permission_mode: Bypass`, `enforce_tool_calls: true`, `yolo: false`; `Fx::policy(agent)` wraps it in ExecutionPolicy with default PolicyInputs. `allowed(p, call)` asserts `is_allow()`. `denied(p, call, pattern)` asserts the call is a Deny whose reason contains `pattern` and returns the reason so a test can also assert `starts_with`. `guard_of(p, call)` returns the denying rule id. `write(path)` builds a canonical Write ToolCall; `bash(cmd)` a Bash ToolCall. Tests are grouped under banner comments by guard and cite the Rule ID in a first-line comment (`// Rule W1.`).
patterns.name: Test fixture and assertion helpers

patterns.description: The most recent small guards (W1, B5, git-metadata) are tested by calling `guard_of` on the Write tool and on shell commands that write (`cp`, `rm`, redirect), looping over agents where the guard must hold for several, and calling `allowed` for a Read of the same file so the guard is shown not to over-block. The git-metadata test also builds a YOLO policy to show YOLO does not override.
patterns.name: A guard test that checks the rule id across tool surfaces and agents

patterns.description: Where the wording matters, tests capture the reason returned by `denied` and assert `starts_with` on the correction clause, in addition to `contains` on a distinguishing phrase. Examples: `r.starts_with("Leave test files to write-test")` (line 244), `r.starts_with("Write your report to \"")` (442), `r.starts_with("Call submit_implementer with status `stuck` ...")` (596), `memory.starts_with("Record lessons with the Memory tool")` (803), `reason.starts_with("Answer with SubagentReply")` (2109), `reason.starts_with("Call SubagentReply")` (2138). No test in ostra-policy checks the 256-character length of any reason.
patterns.name: Asserting the correction comes first

patterns.description: Every Layer 1 reason opens with an imperative that names the allowed alternative (`Write your result in your session dir instead of "{raw}"`, `Use git commands instead of writing`, `Leave "{base}" to {owner}`, `Record lessons with the Memory tool instead of writing`, `Call ProjectCreate for `key` first`, `Drop `{flag}` from the git command`, `Run `{name}` without `{flag}``). The next clause states why the rule exists, usually with 'because' or a colon (`: workspace artifacts belong to the user, so ...`). A closing sentence says where to put what the agent could not do, typically `in your report` or `in your submit call`. The offending path is quoted from the caller's own spelling (`raw`) so the model sees what it typed; the file name alone (`base`) is used for ownership rules; absolute allowed roots are shown through `disp(&roots.repo)`. Messages are built with `format!` and a backslash line continuation inside one string. They follow HANDOVER section 20 (no em dashes, instruction first, then the reason, keep 'because'). Reasons are not hard-capped in Layer 1: many exceed 256 characters (the build-streak and lesson-gate reasons are several hundred), and the Grok adapter shortens them with fit_reason, which keeps the head and the last sentence, so the first sentence must carry the fix and the last sentence must be meaningful on its own.
patterns.name: Denial wording: correction first, then reason with 'because', then optional escape

patterns.description: Grok Build clips deny and ask reasons to 256 characters. The Grok adapter flattens whitespace; if the result is over 256 characters it keeps a head and the final sentence joined by ' … ', falls back to a plain 256-character cut when the head budget is under MIN_HEAD (120).
patterns.name: Grok reason clipping

document.problem: A new Layer 1 guard has to be added to ostra-policy. There is no guard registry: each guard is a free function in guards.rs that returns Option<Denial>, and the order in which guards run is fixed by hand-written call order in ExecutionPolicy::layer1 and in guards::check_write. The first guard that returns a denial wins, so where a new check is placed decides which rule name and message a caller sees. This document records those mechanics, the test harness, and the denial-writing conventions.
document.scope: Task: how Layer 1 guards are defined, ordered, and tested in ostra-policy, and how a denial reason is written. Covers crates/ostra-policy (src and tests), the policy types in ostra-core, the Grok reason clipping, and the docs page that describes the guards. It does not design any new guard, and it does not cover Layer 2 permissions, the bash parser internals, or the executors' handling of a Deny beyond what the docs state.
document.title: Layer 1 guards in ostra-policy

submit.findings_summary: Layer 1 guards are free functions in crates/ostra-policy/src/guards.rs that return Option<Denial>. Each guard has a `pub const` id and builds its Denial through `deny(guard, reason)`, and there is no registry. Order is hand-coded. `ExecutionPolicy::layer1` in policy.rs runs the guards in a fixed sequence with early returns for Report, Document, manage tools and submit_*, and `guards::check_write` holds a second fixed sequence. The first denial wins, and Layer 2 and YOLO never see it. Tests are all integration tests in crates/ostra-policy/tests/policy.rs, built on the Fx fixture and the allowed/denied/guard_of helpers, with a rule-ID comment on each test. Some tests assert `starts_with` on the reason's correction clause. Denial reasons open with the correction naming the allowed alternative, then give the reason with 'because' or a colon, then say where to put what the agent could not do. They do this because Grok clips reasons to 256 characters (`fit_reason` keeps the head and the last sentence). No test in ostra-policy checks reason length.

Whether ostra-tools (Read, Write, Edit) or the sandbox expose file size or line count that a new guard could reuse

docs.task: How a Write tool call reaches the policy as a canonical ToolCall.

asks: Explain how a Write tool call reaches the policy as a canonical ToolCall.

data_flow.step: **Native path, model output.** The provider returns a `ChatResponse`; `run_tools` extracts `(id, name, input)` for each tool_use block (`resp.tool_uses()`), coerces JSON-string arguments only for the submit tool, and runs non-concurrent, non-submit, non-coord tools one at a time. `Write` is not in `is_concurrent`, so it takes the sequential `self.tool(...)` branch.

**Native path, canonicalization.** `tool_end` calls `env.canonical_call(&ToolCall::new(name, input.clone()))`. For `Write` it makes `file_path` absolute with `ToolEnv::resolve` (shell cwd, `~/` expansion, bubblewrap `/tmp` mapping) and leaves `content` untouched. A non-object input is returned unchanged.

**Native path, invalid input.** A `__invalid_json` marker in the input short-circuits to an error result before the policy runs. Otherwise `policy.set_yolo(host.yolo())` and `policy.check(&call)` are called; the call and the decision are emitted as `ExecutionDelta::ToolCall` and `ExecutionDelta::Policy`.

**Harness path, hook arrives.** The harness CLI's PreToolUse hook POSTs a `PolicyRequest {harness, execution, event, payload}` with a bearer token to the server's policy route, which calls `HarnessBridge::handle_policy`. The bridge authorizes the execution token, checks the harness matches, then `adapters::for_harness(req.harness)` selects the adapter.

**Harness path, translation.** `adapter.parse_pre(&payload)` returns `PreParse::Call { call, native }` or `PreParse::Refuse`. Claude: `Write` passes through with the input as sent; Grok: `write`/`write_file`/`Write` -> `Write` with `file_path` normalized from several keys; Agy: `write_to_file` -> `Write` with `file_path` and `content` mapped; Codex: no Write, `apply_patch` -> `ApplyPatch`. Spawn and ask tools are refused here. Unmapped tool names become `Other:<name>`.

**Harness path, decision.** `handle_policy` counts the call (`live.note_tool_call()`), then `decide` rejects a foreign `submit_*` and calls `BridgeServices::policy_check(&live.id, call)`. The server implementation returns early for gateway MCP and manage tools, otherwise calls `ServerBridge::check`, which sets YOLO, denies everything for an inspect (read-only) session, else calls `r.policy.check(call)`, and logs the call and decision. Ask is resolved through `resolve_ask`; the final `Decision::{Allow,Deny}` goes back through `adapter.pre_response`. Note: this path does not call `ToolEnv::canonical_call`, so `file_path` is whatever the harness sent (usually absolute) and relative paths are resolved later by the policy against `start_cwd`.

**Policy, both paths.** `ExecutionPolicy::check` runs `layer1`. For `Write`, `write_paths` returns the single `(resolved PathBuf, raw String)` from `file_path` (resolved by `Roots::resolve` against `start_cwd`: the call's absolute `cwd` field if present, else the repo root). `guards::check_write` runs per target; any denial returns immediately as `PolicyDecision::Deny` with `RuleRef::guard(...)`. `content` is not read by layer 1 or layer 2 today.

**Policy, layer 2.** If layer 1 passes, `layer2` treats `Write` as `Family::Edit`: it evaluates allow/ask/deny rules per target, treats session-dir and temp-dir writes as allowed, allows repo writes in acceptEdits mode, and otherwise falls to the mode default. YOLO turns an Ask into Allow but not a Deny.

**After allow, native only.** `ostra_tools::execute(env, id, &call, ...)` dispatches `"Write"` to `fs::write`, which requires `file_path` and `content`, resolves the path again with `env.resolve`, refuses a directory, and refuses overwriting an existing file the run has not read. Harness Writes are executed by the CLI itself, outside Ostra's tools.

patterns.description: `ToolCall` is a tool-name string plus an untyped `serde_json::Value`. The doc comment in `ostra-core/src/policy.rs` is the schema (`Write {file_path, content}`). The policy reads fields by key (`str_field`), so a field that an adapter does not set is simply absent at check time. Harness adapters translate each CLI's payload into this form before the policy sees it (CLAUDE.md pattern 6).

patterns.description: Each adapter's `parse_pre` maps the CLI's native tool names to canonical ones inside one `match name`. Write-like tools use `with_file_path` (copy the path from whichever key the harness uses into `file_path`, keep the other fields) or build the input by hand (Agy copies `content` too). Unknown tools become `Other:<name>`.

patterns.description: `Run::tool_end` builds the call once with `env.canonical_call`, emits it as `ExecutionDelta::ToolCall`, runs `policy.check`, emits `ExecutionDelta::Policy`, resolves Deny/Ask, then executes the same call. The in-code comment states the reason: relative paths mean the same target in check, approval, and run.

document.problem: Every Write call, native or from a harness CLI, must be reduced to the canonical shape `ToolCall { tool: "Write", input: {file_path, content} }` before `ExecutionPolicy::check` runs. The path to that point differs per executor: native calls go through `ToolEnv::canonical_call`, harness calls go through a per-harness `Adapter::parse_pre`, and the two do not normalize identically (for example, only the native path makes `file_path` absolute before the policy). Anything that wants to inspect a Write's `content` or target in the policy has to know which fields exist at check time on each path.
document.scope: Task: how a Write tool call reaches the policy as a canonical ToolCall. Covers the native executor path, the four harness adapter paths (Claude, Codex, Grok, Agy), the server bridge that owns the harness's ExecutionPolicy, and what the policy does with a Write (layer 1 guards, layer 2 permissions). It does not cover Edit/Bash internals beyond where they share code, the Read tool, the web UI, or any design for a new guard.
document.title: How a Write tool call reaches the policy as a canonical ToolCall

submit.findings_summary: A canonical ToolCall is `{tool: String, input: serde_json::Value}`, and a Write's input is `{file_path, content}`. On the native path, `Run::tool_end` runs `ToolEnv::canonical_call`, which makes `file_path` absolute. It then calls `policy.check`, and only after an allow does it run `fs::write`. On the harness path, the CLI's PreToolUse hook reaches `HarnessBridge::handle_policy`. A per-harness `Adapter::parse_pre` builds the canonical call, `BridgeServices::policy_check` hands it to `ServerBridge::check`, and that calls `ExecutionPolicy::check`. This path does not call `canonical_call`. Claude passes Write through unchanged, Grok and Agy normalize the path (Agy also maps `content`), and Codex has no Write because `apply_patch` becomes `ApplyPatch`. In the policy, layer 1 runs `guards::check_write` per target from `write_paths`, which sees only the resolved path and the raw string, never `content`. Layer 2 treats Write as `Family::Edit`.
